simple-google-analytics-alternative:
Google Analytics 4 is free and very capable. It is also built for marketing teams that live inside Google Ads, build custom reports and model attribution across devices. If you run a docs site, a SaaS landing page or a side project, you probably want answers to a much shorter list of questions.

What most small sites actually need

  • Traffic: page views, unique visitors and sessions over time.
  • Sources: which referrers and UTM campaigns send visitors.
  • Content: top pages, entry pages and exit pages.
  • Actions: a handful of custom events, such as signup_completed or docs_copied.
  • A dashboard you can read in a minute, without building reports first.

If that list covers you, a simpler tool is usually a better fit than GA4.

What you give up compared with GA4

Being honest about trade-offs matters more than feature checklists:

  • Google Ads integration. GA4 connects to Google Ads, Search Ads 360, Display & Video 360 and Search Console. If you buy Google ads and optimise on conversions, that integration is hard to replace.
  • Cross-device user modelling. GA4 uses first-party cookies (_ga, with a default two-year expiry) to distinguish returning users, according to Google's own documentation (as of Oct 2026). Pulzivo sets no cookies and collects no personal data by default, so it does not try to follow one person across devices.
  • Price. GA4's standard tier is free of charge (as of Oct 2026). Pulzivo also has a free plan, but higher volumes are paid.

What you get with a simpler tool

  • Setup in one step. Add a script tag and page views are tracked automatically. Paid plans add automatic click and scroll tracking, sessions, unique visitors and UTM attribution (see pricing for what each plan includes).
  • No cookies, no personal data collected by default. Pulzivo does not set cookies and collects no personal data by default; signed-in users are only identified if you opt in with IDs you supply.
  • A small script. The Pulzivo tracker is about 9KB gzipped.
  • Custom events with one call, from plain HTML or any framework.

Setting up Pulzivo

Create an account, copy your API key from the dashboard, and add the script to your site's <head>:

<script src="https://cdn.pulzivo.com/pulzivo-analytics.min.js"
        data-api-key="YOUR_API_KEY"></script>

Then track the actions you care about:

PulzivoAnalytics('event', 'signup_completed', { plan: 'free' });

It works the same in React, Vue, Angular, Next.js, Svelte or plain HTML because the SDK exposes a global function. See the documentation for configuration options.

Running both side by side

You do not have to switch in one go. Add Pulzivo next to GA4 for a few weeks, check that the numbers tell the same story for your top pages and sources, then decide whether you still need GA4. Expect counts to differ somewhat between any two tools because of ad blockers, bot filtering and different definitions of a session.

Try it

Pulzivo has a free plan (10,000 events/month, 1 website, no credit card). Compare plans on the pricing page or create a free account and add the script tag to your site.
privacy-friendly-analytics-small-sites:
"Privacy-friendly analytics" is used loosely. This checklist is a practical way to decide what to measure on a small site and how to evaluate a tool, including Pulzivo. It is not legal advice: whether you need consent or a banner depends on your jurisdiction and everything else on your site, so check with someone qualified.

1. Decide what questions you need answered

Write down the three to five questions you actually look at. For most small sites they are: how many people visit, where they come from, which pages they read, and whether they complete the one or two actions that matter (signup, download, contact). Anything you will not look at is data you do not need to collect.

2. Prefer aggregate data over individual profiles

Counts per page, per referrer and per country answer the questions above without building a profile of any individual visitor. Pulzivo is designed around this: no cookies, no personal data collected by default.

3. Check how the tool identifies visits

Ask the vendor directly: does the script set cookies? Does it store anything on the device? Does it collect IP addresses, and if so, are they stored? For comparison, Google's documentation states that GA4's JavaScript tags use first-party cookies such as _ga (two-year default expiry) to distinguish users (as of Oct 2026). Pulzivo sets no cookies and collects no personal data by default.

4. Keep custom events free of personal data

The tool is only half the story. If you send an email address or a name as an event property, you have put personal data into your analytics regardless of which vendor you use. Use IDs that mean nothing outside your system, or none at all:

// Good
PulzivoAnalytics('event', 'signup_completed', { plan: 'starter' });

// Avoid
PulzivoAnalytics('event', 'signup_completed', { email: user.email });

5. Look at data retention

Keep data only as long as you use it. On Pulzivo, retention depends on the plan: 30 days on Free, 6 months on Starter, 12 months on Pro and 24 months on Enterprise (see pricing).

6. Weigh script size, but do not obsess

A smaller analytics script is good for page speed, but most of your page weight is usually images, fonts and your own JavaScript. Pulzivo's tracker is about 9KB gzipped. Measure your own pages before and after adding any tool.

7. Update your privacy policy

Whatever tool you choose, describe what you collect and why in plain language on your privacy page.

plausible-vs-pulzivo-vs-ga4:
Plausible, Pulzivo, and Google Analytics 4 all answer "who came to my site?" They are not interchangeable. GA4 is an advertising and analysis suite that happens to include a free tier. Plausible is a cookieless, pageview-metered product aimed at people who want one clear screen. Pulzivo is a cookieless, event-metered product with a free plan and a few product signals on higher plans. This page is how to choose for a small site: a docs site, a SaaS landing page, a side project, or a shop with one main action. It is not a winner's podium.

Start from the question, not the feature grid

Write down the three questions you actually open a dashboard to answer. For most small sites they are: how many people visited, which pages they opened, and whether they did the one action that matters (signup, purchase, docs copy, contact). If your list is longer than that because you buy Google ads, build audiences, or export to a warehouse, you are already in GA4's territory. If your list is that short, a simpler tool will be easier to live with.

What "small site" means here

It means one person, or a tiny team, reads the numbers. There is no analytics specialist whose job is to configure explorations. The site has a handful of important URLs, not a catalog of fifty thousand. You would rather have a number you trust this week than a model of a user you will never look at. That is the audience this comparison is for. A larger marketing org should weigh GA4's advertising links much more heavily than anything below.

Google Analytics 4

Google describes Google Analytics as free of charge. The cost is setup time and the data model. GA4's JavaScript tags use first-party cookies such as _ga to distinguish browsers. That is useful if you need a long-lived client id, and it is a different privacy shape from a tool that sets no cookies. GA4 also connects to Google Ads and can export to BigQuery. If you optimise campaigns inside Google's ad products, or you already have a warehouse job that reads GA4, replacing it is a real project, not a script-tag swap.

The trade-off for a small site is the interface. Reports are built from events, and the default screens are easy to misread until someone has configured key events, internal traffic filters, and the conversions you care about. Many indie developers install GA4, look at it twice, and stop. The tool is capable. It is just built for a job they do not have.

Keep GA4 when any of these are true: you spend money in Google Ads and import conversions back, you need BigQuery, or another tool in your stack already assumes a GA4 property exists. A longer, feature-by-feature pass is on the Pulzivo vs Google Analytics page.

Plausible

Plausible is a well-known cookieless analytics product. It meters monthly pageviews, shows a single dashboard, and publishes an open-source build you can host yourself. It does not try to be GA4. For a site whose questions are traffic, top pages, and referrers, that focus is the point.

Two practical differences matter when you compare it with Pulzivo. First, the meter. Plausible counts pageviews. Pulzivo counts events, and on Pulzivo a page view, a click, and a custom event all draw from the same monthly allowance. The same audience can use more of a Pulzivo plan than it would use of a pageview plan, because clicks are included. Second, the price shape. Plausible's hosted product is paid. Pulzivo has a free plan of 10,000 events a month, one website, and 30 days of retention. The October 2026 price notes, including the Plausible and Fathom figures we checked then, are in Pulzivo vs GA4 vs Plausible: pricing. Prices move, so read that page and the vendors' own pricing before you buy.

Choose Plausible if you want a pageview meter, you are happy on a paid plan, and you do not need Pulzivo's event layer (custom events on the free plan, sessions and UTM attribution from Starter, JavaScript errors on Pro, form abandonment and rage clicks on Enterprise). The side-by-side page is Pulzivo vs Plausible.

Pulzivo

Pulzivo sets no cookies and collects no personal data by default. The core script is about 9KB gzip. You add one script tag, and page views are recorded without a report-building step. The free plan is 10,000 events a month: page views, clicks, custom events, scroll depth, and Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS). Starter (list $9/month, $4.50 for the first 12 months, 100,000 events) adds sessions, unique visitors, and UTM attribution. Pro (list $29/month, $14.50 for the first 12 months) adds performance metrics, opt-in identification with an id you supply, and JavaScript error capture. Enterprise (list $99/month, $49.50 for the first 12 months) adds form abandonment, rage clicks, and dead clicks. 50% off your first 12 months, launch offer until we reach 100 users. The full grid is on the pricing page.

What you give up

  • No Google Ads link and no BigQuery export. If those are requirements, keep GA4.
  • The default visitor id rotates every calendar day. Pulzivo does not, by default, follow one person across days or devices. A stable id exists only if you call identify() on Pro with an id you already have.
  • Because clicks and custom events count toward the same cap as page views, a click-heavy app burns the allowance faster than a quiet blog. Run the free plan for a few weeks and read the real event total before you pick a paid tier.

A simple decision

  • You buy Google ads or you export to BigQuery. Stay on GA4. You can still add Pulzivo beside it to read the site without building reports.
  • You want a paid, pageview-metered, cookieless dashboard and nothing else. Plausible is built for that. Compare the meters before you assume the bills match.
  • You want to start free, send a few custom events, and add sessions or campaign attribution later. Start on Pulzivo Free. Move to Starter when you need UTM attribution or a bounce rate.
  • You want rage clicks, dead clicks, or form abandonment. Those are Enterprise features in Pulzivo, not part of the free plan. If you will never use them, do not pay for them.

Counts will not match across tools. Ad blockers, bot filters, and the definition of a session all move the totals. Run two scripts for a few weeks and compare top pages and top referrers, not the exact visitor number.

track-utm-campaigns:
A UTM campaign is a link you tag so you can tell one visit from another when the referrer is missing or useless. Email apps, mobile apps, and many social apps strip the referrer. Without tags, those visits land in "direct" and you cannot tell a newsletter from a stranger typing the URL. The tags are five query parameters. The hard part is naming them the same way every time, so the report does not split one campaign into six rows.

The five parameters

Only the first three are required for a useful report. The last two are optional and worth using when you are testing more than one creative.

  • utm_source is where the click came from: newsletter, google, linkedin, partner-site.
  • utm_medium is the channel type: email, cpc, social, referral.
  • utm_campaign is the effort: november-launch, docs-refresh, black-friday. One name per effort, reused across sources.
  • utm_term is the paid keyword, when you have one. Skip it on email and organic social.
  • utm_content tells creatives apart: hero, footer, text-link.

A link you can read out loud

This is a newsletter link to a pricing page. Source, medium, campaign, and which button:

https://example.com/pricing?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=november-launch&utm_content=hero

Build that URL in the UTM campaign URL builder. It runs in the browser and does not upload the address. Pick a preset (Google, email, LinkedIn, and the others on that page) when you want a conventional medium, then edit the campaign name. Copy the result into the email tool or the ad.

Naming rules that keep the report to one row

Analytics tools treat Newsletter, newsletter, and news_letter as three sources. Pick one spelling and write it down. These rules are enough for a small site:

  • Lowercase only. Hyphens, not spaces or underscores.
  • One canonical source per place. The Sunday email is always newsletter, never mailchimp one week and email the next. Put the tool name in the campaign if you need it (november-launch), not in the source.
  • Medium is the channel, not the tool. email, cpc, social, referral. Pulzivo groups cpc, ppc, and paid as Paid Search, email as Email, and social as Social Media. If you invent utm_medium=newsletter, you lose that grouping and the row sits on its own.
  • Campaign names stay stable for the life of the effort. Do not append the send date to the campaign if you want the three sends added together. Put the date in utm_content (nov-21) when you need to split them.
  • Do not tag links inside your own site. An internal link with UTMs overwrites the campaign that actually brought the visitor. Tag the link that leaves the other site, the ad, or the email, and stop there.

Write a one-page cheat sheet

Before the next launch, list the sources you really use. A typical indie list is short: newsletter / email, google / cpc, linkedin / social, docs-partner / referral. Share that list with anyone who sends a link, including yourself in two months. The builder presets cover the common pairs. The cheat sheet covers the campaign names, which are yours.

What shows up in Pulzivo

The script reads utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, utm_term, and utm_content when it loads, including on the first page of a visit. That matters on a React, Angular, or Next.js app, because the router sometimes strips the query during boot. The landing snapshot is taken before that happens. Installation is the same script tag as the rest of the product. The steps are in the documentation.

On the dashboard, UTM and attribution reports are part of Starter and above, not the free plan. The free plan is still 10,000 events a month and records page views, clicks, custom events, scroll depth, and Web Vitals, so you can install now and read campaign rows after you move to Starter. You can also turn UTM capture off for a site with setPreferences({ utm_attribution: false }) if you have a reason to drop the parameters. Plan limits and the Starter feature list are on the pricing page.

Check one real click before the campaign goes out

Send the tagged URL to yourself, open it, and confirm the page view carries the five values you typed. Fix the spelling in the email tool, not in the report, if a source looks wrong. A report cannot merge linked-in and linkedin after the fact without an export and a spreadsheet.

Keep a note of the campaign names you have already used. Reusing november-launch on the next email adds to the same row, which is what you want when it is still that launch. Starting a fresh name, november-launch-2, splits the history. Decide that before the second send, not after you have two half-rows.

What UTMs will not do

They do not identify a person. They describe the link. They do not survive if the visitor copies the address bar and deletes the query, and they do not repair a campaign that used a different name last month. They also do not replace a custom event. "Clicked the ad" is a UTM. "Finished signup" is PulzivoAnalytics('event', 'signup_completed', { plan: 'free' }), which is available on every plan, including Free.

Tag the next email with one consistent source, medium, and campaign. When you want those rows in the dashboard, Starter is the plan that includes them. Start free if you do not have an account yet, and use the builder for the URL so a missing parameter does not ship.
core-web-vitals-for-site-owners:
Core Web Vitals are three field measurements of how a page feels: how long until the main content appears, how quickly the page reacts to a tap or a click, and how much the layout jumps while it loads. Google publishes them, search tools surface them, and they are easy to misread if you only have a lab score from your own laptop. This is the owner’s version: what each number means, which cutoffs are "good", and how to get the numbers from real visits.

The three numbers

LCP, largest contentful paint

LCP is the time until the largest visible piece of content is painted. On a marketing page that is usually the hero image or the main headline block. On a docs page it is often the title plus the first paragraph. Google's published guidance treats 2.5 seconds or less as good and more than 4.0 seconds as poor. Between those, the rating is "needs improvement". Pulzivo uses those same cutoffs.

A slow LCP is usually one of a short list: a hero image that is larger than the slot it sits in, a font that blocks the first paint, a server that is slow to send HTML, or a script in the head that runs before the content. You do not need a performance project to test the first one. Serve a reasonably sized image, give it width and height, and load it early.

INP, interaction to next paint

INP measures how long the page takes to show the next frame after a visitor clicks, taps, or presses a key. It replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital. Good is 200 milliseconds or less. Poor is more than 500 milliseconds. The number people feel is the worst of the interactions on that page, not the average of the easy ones.

A bad INP is almost always JavaScript. A click handler that sorts a large list, a third-party widget that locks the main thread, or a framework re-render of the whole page will push it over the line. The fix is to do less work on the interaction, not to buy a faster laptop. Lab tools on a developer machine often miss this, because the machine is idle and the page is warm.

CLS, cumulative layout shift

CLS measures unexpected movement of content. Good is 0.1 or less. Poor is more than 0.25. The classic causes are an image or an ad without reserved space, a banner injected above the article after load, and a web font that swaps and reflows the paragraph. A shift the visitor caused, such as opening an accordion, is not the problem you are hunting. The problem is the page moving while they are trying to read or tap.

Reserve the space. Put width and height on images, or use CSS aspect-ratio. Do not insert a cookie-style bar or a promo above the content after the first paint. If a late element has to appear, put it below the fold or over a placeholder of the same size.

Field data, not a single Lighthouse run

Lighthouse and PageSpeed Insights are useful lab checks. They load the page once, on one device profile, and tell you what might be slow. Core Web Vitals, as Google uses them for ranking reports, are field data: the experience of real visitors, typically looked at as a 75th percentile. One fast run on your office connection does not mean the 75th percentile visitor on a phone had a good LCP.

Pulzivo records LCP, INP, and CLS in the browser with a PerformanceObserver and sends them as Web Vital events. The dashboard rates the 75th percentile against the cutoffs above. Web Vitals are on the free plan, along with page views, clicks, custom events, and scroll depth. You do not need Starter or above to see them. The plan grid is on the pricing page, and the install is the same script tag described in the documentation.

How to read the card

  • Look at the 75th percentile, not the average. The average hides the slow quarter of visits.
  • Read it per page. A homepage with a giant image and a docs page full of text will not share an LCP.
  • Ignore a rating with a tiny sample. A handful of visits is not a distribution. Wait until the page has real traffic before you redesign around one red number.
  • Compare a page to itself over time. A deploy that adds a chat widget is easier to spot that way than a comparison against an unrelated site.

A practical order of fixes

If LCP is poor, start with the largest element. In the browser's performance panel, find which node was the LCP element, then shrink it or load it sooner. If INP is poor, record a click on the slow control with the performance panel and look for a long task. If CLS is poor, reload the page and watch what jumps. Those three checks solve more owner-facing problems than a generic "improve your score" pass.

Third-party scripts, including analytics, sit on the same thread. Pulzivo's core script is about 9KB gzip, which is small next to a tag manager full of pixels, but it is not free. If you are chasing INP, measure before and after you add any script. The features page lists what the free script records automatically, so you can see whether you still need the other tags.

What this will not tell you

Web Vitals do not say whether the copy is clear, whether the form is too long, or whether anyone finished signup. They say whether the page was slow, sluggish, or jumpy for real visits. Pair them with the page list and, when you have them, with scroll depth. A fast page that nobody scrolls is a content problem. A slow page that people still finish is a performance problem you can schedule.

Install the script, open a page you actually care about, and read LCP, INP, and CLS at the 75th percentile before you change the design. The free plan includes those metrics. Start free and give it a few days of real traffic before you treat a lab score as the answer.
what-cookieless-analytics-means:
"Cookieless analytics" has become a label. Vendors use it to mean different things, and a reader can easily walk away thinking it means "we store nothing" or "you never need to think about consent." Neither of those follows from the phrase. This page is the careful version: what the word actually describes, what it does not decide for you, and how Pulzivo implements it. It is not legal advice. Whether your site needs a banner depends on your jurisdiction and on everything else you load, not on a slogan.

What the word refers to

A cookie is a small name-value pair the browser stores and sends back to the site on later requests. Analytics products have used one, often for a year or two, as a client id so they can tell a returning browser from a new one. "Cookieless" means the analytics script does not set that kind of cookie. It does not mean the product has no identifier at all, and it does not mean the browser holds nothing.

Cookie, localStorage, and memory

localStorage is a different browser API. It is not sent automatically with every request the way a cookie is, and it does not expire on its own. A script can still keep a random id there. sessionStorage lasts for the tab. A value held only in memory disappears on refresh. A product can be cookieless and still use one or more of those. If a vendor says "cookieless," the useful follow-up is: what, if anything, do you write to the device, how long does it live, and does it identify a person?

Google's documentation describes GA4's JavaScript tags as using first-party cookies such as _ga. That is a cookie-based design, whatever else the product does. The comparison is on the Pulzivo vs Google Analytics page, including where GA4 remains the better fit.

What Pulzivo does

Pulzivo's script does not set an analytics cookie. By default it keeps an anonymous visitor id in localStorage, stamped with the calendar day. On a new day it mints a new id. Nothing in that value ties today's visits to yesterday's. A session id, also in localStorage, rolls over after a period of inactivity so one sitting is separate from the whole day. The mechanics, including Do Not Track, Global Privacy Control, and optOut(), are written up on the cookieless analytics page. This article is the definition. That page is the implementation.

No personal data is collected by default. The ordinary event is a page path, a title, a referrer, and the rotating id. An email is sent only if your code calls identify() or sets an email, and that path is opt-in. A permanent id (pz_uid) is written only after identify() on the Pro plan, using an id you supply. Until you do that, there is no stable visitor key.

What you can still measure

  • On the free plan: page views, clicks, custom events, scroll depth, and Core Web Vitals. The allowance is 10,000 events a month.
  • On Starter: sessions, unique visitors within the way the product defines them, and UTM attribution.
  • On Pro: opt-in identification and JavaScript errors.
  • On Enterprise: form abandonment, rage clicks, and dead clicks.

Daily rotation means the free product cannot, by itself, connect yesterday's anonymous reader to today's signup. If you need that, pass your own id on Pro. If you do not, you still have page, source, and action counts. The plan list is on the pricing page.

What the label does not decide

Cookieless is not a statement about the law. Some regions regulate localStorage and similar storage, not only cookies. A product that sets no cookie can still be something you need to describe in a privacy policy, and it can still sit next to other scripts on your page that do set cookies. Pulzivo does not promise that you can skip a banner. It promises not to set a cookie and not to collect personal data by default. The rest is a question for someone qualified to look at your site.

Cookieless is also not the same as "anonymous in every sense." The rotating id distinguishes browsers for a day so the dashboard is not a single total. IP addresses may be used in transit to derive a coarse location and then not stored as a personal profile. Read the vendor's actual policy. A marketing sentence is not the policy.

Questions worth asking any vendor

  • Does the script call the cookie API? If the answer is no, ask what it writes to localStorage or sessionStorage and when that value changes.
  • Is there a long-lived id by default, or only after you pass one?
  • Can a visitor turn collection off, and does the script honor Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control?
  • What do you do with an email if the customer sends one by accident inside an event property? Pulzivo redacts email-shaped strings. You should still not put an email in a custom property.

A plain description you can reuse

For a privacy page, a precise sentence beats a slogan: the analytics script sets no cookies and collects no personal data by default. It stores an anonymous id that changes each calendar day, plus a session id, in localStorage. A name, an email, or a stable id is sent only if the site opts in and supplies the value. Adjust that sentence if you have called identify(), because then you are sending an id you chose.

The core script is about 9KB gzip. That size is unrelated to the cookie question, but it is the script you are describing. If you want to see the default payload on your own site, start free. The free plan is 10,000 events a month, and you can read the cookieless page linked above before you turn any opt-in identity on.
rage-clicks-and-dead-clicks:
A rage click is a visitor hitting the same control over and over because nothing seemed to happen. A dead click is a click that does not navigate, does not scroll the page, and is not a click into a form field. Both are clues about the interface, not about the person's mood. Used carefully, they tell you which button, link, or card is wasting a visit. Used carelessly, they send you chasing a modal that was working fine.

How Pulzivo detects them

Rage clicks and dead clicks are Enterprise features. They are not on Free, Starter, or Pro. The optional extras script, which also carries form tracking, loads only when the plan enables those modules. The core script stays the smaller file (about 9KB gzip) on plans that do not need them. The grid is on the pricing page.

Rage click: three clicks in one second

The extras script counts a rage click when the same element receives three clicks within one second. "Same element" is the tag name plus its id plus its class list, so two identical buttons with no id can be grouped together, and a button with an id stays distinct. When the threshold is hit, Pulzivo records a rage_click event with the element, the visible text, the page, and the click count, then resets the counter so one frustrated burst does not become a stream of duplicate events.

That definition is narrower than "the visitor seemed annoyed." Three deliberate clicks on a toolbar icon, spaced a second apart, do not qualify. Three clicks in a single second on a button that did not respond do. The docs section that introduces the event is Rage clicks and Web Vitals.

Dead click: nothing visible changed

On each click, the script notes the URL and the scroll position, then checks again 500 milliseconds later. If the URL is the same, the scroll position is the same, and the target is not an input, textarea, select, or label, it records a dead_click with the element, its text, the page, and the href if it had one. Form fields are excluded because focusing a field does not change the URL or the scroll position, and that click was not dead.

This check has a known blind spot. A control that opens a modal, toggles a menu, or updates a panel in place, without changing the URL and without moving the scroll position, can look dead. Treat a dead click as a lead. Confirm it by using the control yourself. If the modal opened, the detector was wrong about that element, and you can ignore that row.

How to work a list of them

Sort by count, not by how dramatic the label sounds. A control with dozens of rage clicks on one page is a broken or slow button. A single dead click on a footer link is noise. For each row you keep, write down the page, the element text, and what you expected to happen.

  • The control does nothing. The handler is missing, the button is disabled without an explanation, or a overlay is intercepting the click. Fix the handler or remove the control.
  • The control is slow. The work ran, but not within a second, so the visitor clicked again. Show a pending state on the first click and ignore further clicks until it finishes. Pair this with Interaction to Next Paint if the whole page feels stuck. That metric is on every plan, including Free, and is covered in Core Web Vitals for site owners.
  • The control looks clickable and is not. A card, a heading, or an icon styled like a button will collect dead clicks from people who believed it was a link. Either make it a link or restyle it so it does not invite a click.
  • The click worked and the detector could not see it. In-page UI, as above. Do not "fix" a working menu because a heuristic flagged it.

Give elements a stable id

The grouping key uses the id when there is one. A button with id="checkout" shows up as its own row. A set of anonymous <div class="card"> elements collapse together, and you cannot tell which card was the problem. Add ids to the controls you care about. You do not need an id on every span.

What to do with the event

Open the events list and filter to rage_click or dead_click. The text and the page are usually enough to reproduce the issue without a recording. Fix the worst page first, deploy, and see whether that row's count drops. A count that stays high after a fix means the fix missed the element people are actually hitting, often a different button with similar text.

Do not page the whole team for these events. They are a weekly review, next to 404s and the slowest Web Vitals. If you are on a plan below Enterprise, you will not have these two events. Scroll depth, click tracking, and Web Vitals are on the free plan and will still show you a page people do not scroll and a page that is slow. Rage and dead clicks are the extra signal when the plan includes them.

If you already know a control is misbehaving, you do not need to wait for a quota. Reproduce it, fix it, and use the events afterward to see whether the burst stopped. When you want them recorded, Enterprise is the plan that includes them. Start free if you still need the base script in place. The extras file is fetched only after the plan turns the module on.
measure-form-abandonment:
Form abandonment is a form someone started and did not submit before they left the page. It is a narrower idea than "they did not convert." A visitor who never focused a field did not abandon the form. They ignored it. The number worth acting on is the gap between people who started and people who submitted, plus which fields they actually touched.

What Pulzivo records

Form tracking is an Enterprise feature, in the same optional extras script as rage clicks and dead clicks. It is not on Free, Starter, or Pro. The core script does not include it. See the pricing page for the plan that does.

The four events

  • form_start fires the first time a visitor focuses an input, textarea, or select in that form. The payload has the form id and the page.
  • form_field_interaction fires on each focus. The field name is the element's name, or its id if there is no name, or the input type if it has neither. This is the event that tells you which fields were touched.
  • form_submit fires on the form's submit event, with how long it had been since the start and the list of field names that were focused.
  • form_abandon fires when the page is unloading, and only if the form was started and at least one field was focused and the form was not submitted. It includes the form id, the page, how many distinct fields were focused, and how long the visitor spent.

Read that last event carefully. fieldsCompleted is the number of distinct fields the visitor focused. The event's totalFields is that same count. The script does not walk the form and count every input that exists. It cannot tell you "they stopped at field 4 of 9" unless you look at the focus events and you know how the form is built. The focus events carry the field names. The abandon event tells you the form was left unfinished.

Name the form and the fields

If the form has no id and no name, every such form on the site is recorded as unknown-form and you cannot tell the signup form from the contact form. Set id or name on the <form>, and set name on each field you want to recognise. name="email" is readable in the event list. A generated id is not. The install for the base script is in the documentation. The extras file is loaded by that script only when the plan includes form tracking.

A weekly review that stays short

Pull two numbers per form: starts, and submits. Abandonment for the week is starts minus submits, for forms that were actually focused. Then open the field-focus events for the form with the worst gap and see which names appear often on abandoned visits and rarely on submitted ones. That field is the one to look at first. Common causes:

  • The field asks for something the visitor does not have ready (a company size, a phone number, a VAT id) with no explanation of why.
  • Validation runs late. The visitor fills five fields, hits submit, and the first field errors in a way that looks like the form ate their work.
  • The form is longer than the decision. A newsletter form with six fields will lose people who would have given an email.
  • The submit control does not look like it worked, so they leave. That can also show up as a rage click on the button. Rage clicks are Enterprise as well, and the way they are counted is in Rage clicks and dead clicks.

Fixes that match the evidence

If almost nobody focuses the form, the problem is the page, not the fields. Move the form, or cut the paragraph above it. If they focus the first field and leave, the first field is the problem. If they focus every field and still do not submit, look at the button, the error text, and anything the submit handler does before the request returns. Do not add a motivational headline. Remove a field, name the error, and keep the values in place when validation fails.

Do not put an email address or a name into a custom event property to "understand" who left. The field-focus event already has the field name, which is what you need. Sending the value turns an anonymous product metric into personal data you did not have to collect. Pulzivo collects no personal data by default. Keep it that way unless you have a separate, deliberate reason and a place to document it.

What you can learn without Enterprise

On the free plan you still have page views, clicks, and custom events. A single signup_completed event, which you send yourself on a successful response, tells you how many people finished. It does not tell you who started and stopped, and it does not name the field. That is the gap form tracking fills, and it is why the feature sits on Enterprise rather than on the free script. If you only have one form and a handful of visits, watch a few people use it, or use it yourself with the network panel open. You do not need a metric to delete two unnecessary fields.

When the form is busy enough that you cannot watch it, the events above are the record. Start free to get the base script on the site. Turn on form tracking when you are on Enterprise and the form id is in place, then read starts against submits before you redesign the whole page.
bounce-rate-without-ga4:
Bounce rate is the share of sessions that ended without a second page view. It is a blunt number. A docs article that answered the question, a blog post that was read to the end, and a broken landing page can all "bounce." GA4 moved its default language toward engagement rate, and the two percentages are not mirrors of each other. If you are reading Pulzivo instead of GA4, you need the definition Pulzivo actually uses, and a better set of questions than "is the rate high?"

The definition in Pulzivo

A session counts as bounced when it has one page view. The bounce rate is that count divided by the number of sessions in the range. Sessions, and the bounce rate that comes from them, are on Starter and above ("session and bounce rate analytics" on the pricing page). They are not on the free plan. The free plan still has page views, clicks, scroll depth, and Core Web Vitals, which are often the more honest signals. More on those below.

This is not Google's engaged-session definition. Google documents an engaged session as one that lasts longer than 10 seconds, or includes a key event, or has two or more page views. A ten-second visit with one page view can be "engaged" in GA4 and "bounced" in Pulzivo. If you are comparing a GA4 engagement rate to a Pulzivo bounce rate, you are comparing two different questions. Do not expect them to add up to 100 percent. The practical difference between the products is on the GA4 alternative page.

Why a high bounce rate is sometimes the goal

A recipe, a changelog, a support answer, and a blog post are often successful when the visitor reads one URL and leaves. They came for that page. A second page view would mean they did not find it. On those URLs, a high bounce rate plus a deep scroll is a good outcome. A high bounce rate plus a few percent of scroll is a page that failed in the first screen.

The opposite is a signup flow or a pricing page. There you want another step: the account form, the docs, the checkout. A high bounce rate on those URLs is a reason to look at the first screen, the load time, and the next link, not a reason to panic about the sitewide average.

What to read instead of one sitewide rate

Split the question by page type before you look at any percentage.

  • Did they stay on the page? Scroll depth is on the free plan and is reported with the page exit. A pricing page whose typical scroll is under a quarter of the document is a first-screen problem. A docs page with a deep scroll and one page view is probably fine.
  • Did the page feel broken? LCP, INP, and CLS are on the free plan. A bounced visit on a page with a poor LCP is a speed problem wearing a bounce costume. The cutoffs and the way to read the 75th percentile are in Core Web Vitals for site owners.
  • Did they do the thing? Send one custom event for the action that matters, such as signup_completed or docs_copied. Custom events are on every plan, including Free. A page with a high bounce rate and a steady stream of that event is doing its job.
  • Did they come from somewhere that promised something else? A campaign that lands on the wrong URL will bounce. UTM attribution, which tells you the campaign, is on Starter, the same plan as the bounce rate. Fix the landing URL before you rewrite the page.

How to use the bounce rate once you have it

On Starter, read bounce rate per entry page, not as one number for the whole property. Sort entry pages by sessions, then look at bounce rate only for pages with enough sessions that a couple of visits cannot swing it. Compare a page to its own previous period. A jump after a deploy is actionable. A stable 70 percent on a blog you have not touched is probably the shape of that content.

Ignore the sitewide rate in a status meeting. It mixes the docs (fine to leave) with the signup page (not fine to leave) and produces a number nobody can act on. If someone asks for it, give them the entry pages instead.

A short routine

Once a week, open the three entry pages that matter: the homepage or the campaign landing page, the pricing page, and the one article or docs URL you are currently sending people to. For each, note sessions if you are on Starter, scroll depth, and whether the custom event fired. If the landing page is slow, check LCP before you touch the copy. If scroll is deep and the event never fires, the ending of the page is the problem, not the headline. If bounce is high and scroll is deep on a blog post, leave it alone.

Pulzivo's session is not a cross-device identity. The default visitor id rotates each calendar day, and a session ends after inactivity. A person who reads an article, leaves, and comes back tomorrow is a new session, and the first of those can be a bounce even though they returned. That is another reason not to treat the rate as a verdict on the content.

Where this leaves the free plan

You can learn a lot before you have a bounce rate. Page views tell you which URLs are used. Scroll depth tells you whether those visits got past the hero. A custom event tells you whether the action happened. Web Vitals tell you whether the page was slow or jumpy. The bounce rate, when you move to Starter, adds the "one page and done" cut on top of that. It does not replace it.

The free plan is 10,000 events a month, one site, no card. Start free, put the script on the pages you are judging, and read scroll and the one custom event for a week before you adopt a bounce target you found on someone else's blog.
